title: Streaming is becoming cultural discovery infrastructure, but platform value and local cultural benefits remain jointly contested
source_unit: Digital Media Association 2026 Annual Report, using MusicWatch consumer research
geography: United States plus Canada, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico; comparative consumer streaming and music-culture findings

observations.period: December 2025–February 2026; U.S. music-streaming engagement and value

denominator.unit: U.S. internet-using respondents ages 13–70 in MusicWatch research

daily_streaming.unit: percent listening to streaming services every day

paid_daily_streaming.unit: percent of paid subscribers listening every day

service_affection.unit: percent saying they like or love their streaming service

service_value.unit: percent describing their service as good, very good, or excellent value

platform_value.value: streaming is experienced as a high-frequency, high-value cultural service rather than only a distribution channel

observations.method: MusicWatch survey for DIMA among 3,555 U.S. respondents ages 13–70, weighted and projected to the U.S. internet-using population by age, gender, ethnicity, income, and region.
observations.uncertainty: DIMA represents major music-streaming services and the report is industry-sponsored; reported satisfaction and value are not independent measures of artist compensation, market concentration, affordability for non-users, or long-term retention.
observations.subgroup: U.S. streamers, paid subscribers, non-paying listeners, age cohorts, and listeners with different spending and format mixes.
observations.counterinterpretation: High satisfaction can coexist with subscription fatigue, unequal access, low artist income, algorithmic dependence, and limited bargaining power over platform terms.

observations.period: December 2025–February 2026; U.S. music spending and artist connection

denominator.unit: U.S. internet-using respondents ages 13–70 in MusicWatch research

artist_connection.unit: percent saying streaming improves their connection to artists and music they love

annual_recorded_music_spend.unit: approximate U.S. dollars spent annually by the average streamer on recorded music

paid_subscriber_spend.unit: approximate U.S. dollars spent annually by paid on-demand subscribers on recorded music

five_year_change.unit: percent more recorded-music spending than five years earlier

consumption_currency.value: platform engagement converts into artist connection and broader music spending, but the report does not establish how value is distributed across artists or listeners

observations.method: MusicWatch expenditure and attitude measures summarized in DIMA’s annual report.
observations.uncertainty: The spending figures are report estimates and averages; they do not identify household budget tradeoffs, artist-level payouts, distributional incidence, or causation from streaming to spending.
observations.subgroup: Average streamers, paid on-demand subscribers, artists, songwriters, labels, platforms, and households with different disposable income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising music spending may reflect price changes, format substitution, higher-income users, or more complete measurement rather than broad-based consumer surplus or artist prosperity.

observations.period: December 2025–February 2026; music discovery and cultural memory

denominator.unit: U.S. internet-using respondents ages 13–70 in MusicWatch research

streaming_discovery.unit: percent naming streaming as a main source for discovering new music

social_discovery.unit: percent naming social media as a main source for discovering new music

playlist_tool.unit: percent using playlists as a discovery feature

recommendation_tool.unit: percent using recommendations as a discovery feature

back_catalogue.unit: percent of streamers using streaming to discover older songs

memory_route.value: streaming expands both novelty and cultural memory by making older catalogs searchable and recommender-visible

observations.method: Music discovery questions covering sources, platform features, new releases, and older songs.
observations.uncertainty: Discovery is self-reported and does not show whether recommendations broaden taste, reinforce existing preferences, or change artist income and cultural participation.
observations.subgroup: Listeners across generations, with different preferences for homepage exploration, playlists, recommendation systems, radio-style features, and social discovery.
observations.counterinterpretation: Greater catalog access can increase choice while making attention more dependent on platform ranking, metadata, licensing, and recommendation design.

observations.period: December 2025–February 2026; comparative streaming and local-culture route

denominator.unit: approximately 1,000 respondents each in Canada, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico

comparative_scope.value: parallel MusicWatch studies were conducted in Canada, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico with country-specific weighting

global_discovery.value: the report describes streaming as a route to new genres and artists across borders, alongside country-specific listening and spending patterns

local_culture.value: the report examines whether streaming helps preserve, promote, and discover local culture and artists

regulatory_meaning.value: consumer views of platform access and government oversight differ across markets, making streaming both a cultural interface and a policy object

observations.method: Parallel country studies of music listening, discovery, spending, AI-generated music, local culture, and government oversight.
observations.uncertainty: The comparative samples are country-specific online studies and the source is a trade association report; cross-country percentages should not be treated as fully equivalent without the underlying questionnaires and weighting details.
observations.subgroup: Listeners in Canada, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico, including paid and unpaid users, local-artist audiences, and people with different views of regulation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Platform reach can support local discovery while concentrating cultural gatekeeping, revenue, data, and policy leverage in a small number of global services.

related_sources.claim: DIMA report index and Streaming Forward research context.
Full DIMA 2026 report with U.S. and comparative music-streaming findings.
Complementary consumption-side source on streaming growth, genre diversification, and library viewing.

boundary: This record adds a platform-to-culture and platform-to-consumption route across engagement, spending, discovery, back-catalogue use, local culture, AI-generated music, and regulation. It does not treat industry-sponsored satisfaction as independent welfare evidence, infer artist-level distribution, or establish that streaming causes cultural diversity, local-artist success, or consumer surplus.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official DIMA 2026 Annual Report PDF and DIMA release reviewed for U.S. and comparative samples, engagement, value, spending, discovery, back-catalogue, local-culture, AI, and oversight claims.
